name: Sequential buffer allocator (seq_buf_allocator) with std::vector and Vector<T,A>
listed_description: Stateful traditional allocator that hands out memory from a pre-allocated stack buffer in sequence and never frees individual blocks, used with std::vector and the book's own allocator-aware Vector<T,A>.
claim_text: Book says the test shows interesting performance with the sequential buffer allocator, and the book's Vector<T,A> outperforms std::vector<T,A>; no numbers printed.
book_benchmark: 500,000 push_back insertions of a one-int struct after reserve, timed in microseconds with std::chrono, default allocator against the sequential buffer allocator, for std::vector and the book's Vector. Compiler, flags and CPU not stated, results not printed.
found_in: book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 14, Example usage - a sequential buffer allocator (companion code in chapter14)

name: Vector<T> with allocation separated from construction
listed_description: Book's teaching Vector<T> rewritten to take raw memory with malloc and construct elements in place with the uninitialized memory algorithms, avoiding wasted default construction before std::fill.
claim_text: Naive version default-constructs elements that are then overwritten; the rewrite aims to get closer to std::vector performance by doing minimal work.
book_benchmark: No timings in this chunk; qualitative argument only, with the full implementation in the companion repository.
found_in: book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 12 end, A more efficient Vector<T> and Using low-level standard facilities

name: Trivial relocation (std::relocate / is_trivially_relocatable, C++26)
listed_description: Replace move-then-destroy of elements during container growth with a single memcpy for trivially relocatable types, via a trait and a relocate function adopted into C++26 in February 2025 (proposals by O'Dwyer, Wang, Meredith and Gill).
claim_text: Reported to give considerable benefits, with some claiming up to 30% speedup in common cases; experimental, more benchmarks expected.
book_benchmark: None run by the book; the 30% figure is cited second-hand with no workload, compiler or CPU. The book's resize() example compares uninitialized_move plus destroy against memcpy-style relocation.
guessed_baseline: std::uninitialized_move followed by std::destroy (move-and-destroy reallocation in std::vector)
found_in: book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 15, Trivial relocation

name: std::pmr monotonic_buffer_resource and pool resources
listed_description: Standard C++17 polymorphic memory resources: monotonic buffer over a stack array, synchronized and unsynchronized pool resources, with PMR containers propagating the resource to nested strings.
claim_text: Book says PMR is fast enough for most needs, but traditional allocators give more control over execution time and object size.
book_benchmark: No timings; examples show a stack buffer resource, a tracing resource and nested propagation only.
found_in: book: C++ Memory Management (2025), ch. 14, Polymorphic memory resource allocators and Upsides and costs
